samples.summary: The auth gate's `/login` redirect is a `push`, not a `replace`, so it is routed through the one navigator method this delta still guards — contradicting the exemption's stated premise and making the session-expiry redirect refusable (and then permanently swallowed) by a "Stay".
samples.evidence: navigation-guard-provider.tsx:148-158 now guards only `push`, and the comment justifies it with "`replace` is how this app corrects the URL on its own behalf — … `PrivateRoute` sending you to /login"; docs/design/sync-status.md repeats the claim ("`PrivateRoute` sends you to `/login`" listed under the replace exemption) and docs/tasks/active/20260916-nav-guard-unsent-edits-lessons.md states "`PrivateRoute` renders `<Navigate to="/login" replace />`". The actual code is `<Navigate to="/login" />` (PrivateRoute.tsx:32) with no `replace` prop, and react-router's `useNavigate` dispatches `(!!options.replace ? navigator.replace : navigator.push)(path, …)` — the very call shape the provider's own comment at line 141-142 quotes. So the unauthenticated redirect lands on the guarded `push` path. Vector: a user editing a document with unsent edits (`mayHaveUnsent` true, so `SyncStatusChip` has registered a guard) has their session expire; react-query refetches `fetchMe` on window focus (`retry: false`), `me` becomes undefined, `PrivateRoute` renders `<Navigate to="/login" />`. If the guard is still in `guardsRef` at that instant, `push` holds the redirect in `pendingRef` and shows the Stay/Leave dialog; clicking Stay clears it and the effect that issued it never re-runs (the query state does not change again), so the browser keeps displaying the private URL with a dead session — exactly the "swallowed for good" hazard the delta claims to have eliminated, applied to the auth gate. I could not close the chain: React commits a deleted subtree's passive cleanups (the chip's `register` teardown, use-navigation-guard.ts:56) before newly mounted effects, so in the common case the guard set is already empty when `<Navigate>`'s effect fires, and the `<Outlet/>` subtree unmounts regardless, so no private data stays rendered and no server-side authorization is bypassed. `PublicRoute.tsx:21` has the same missing `replace`. Fix is one prop (`replace`) on both, which also makes the code match the comment and the design doc.

samples.summary: The forced sign-out redirect after a 401 is a full-page `window.location.href`, which the PR's `beforeunload` guard makes user-cancelable — the session is already destroyed server-side but the user can keep the private page on screen.
samples.evidence: `fetchWithAuth` on an unrefreshable 401 calls `await logout({ redirect: false, … })` (auth.ts:154) and then `redirectTo("/login")` → `window.location.href = path` (auth.ts:30, 159). A full-document navigation fires `beforeunload`, and `SyncStatusChip` registers a `beforeunload` handler that calls `event.preventDefault()` whenever `hasUnsentEdits()` (sync-status-chip.tsx:92-103), so the browser shows its native "Leave site?" prompt and a user who answers "Cancel" stays on the authenticated route with the session cookie already cleared — the app continues rendering the document and the Yorkie connection is untouched, with no client-side re-check to tear it down. No new data is exposed that was not already on the screen and the backend still rejects every subsequent request, so this is hardening rather than a bypass. Noted because the delta's whole premise is which redirects must be unrefusable, and this one — the actual session-expiry redirect — bypasses the navigator seam entirely and is refusable through the other guard the PR adds. The `beforeunload` guard itself predates this delta.

verdict.reason: The factual premise checks out — PrivateRoute.tsx:32 is `<Navigate to="/login" />` without `replace`, PublicRoute.tsx:21 likewise, and navigation-guard-provider.tsx:148-157 guards only `push` while its comment cites PrivateRoute as a `replace` case. But there is no security impact under this lens. The access-control decision itself (PrivateRoute.tsx:22-33) is unchanged and cannot be bypassed by navigation: when `me` is falsy the entire private subtree is simply not rendered, and App.tsx:128-176 shows every private route lives inside that `<Outlet/>` (including Layout at App.tsx:129), so a held-back redirect yields a blank page, not exposed data. The only guard registrant is sync-status-chip.tsx:115 (sole consumer of useNavigationGuard, use-navigation-guard.ts:46-57), which sits inside that same subtree and whose passive cleanup removes the guard in the same commit — the reviewer concedes the chain does not close. Server-side authorization is independent (App.tsx:152-155 states the reviewer allowlist is enforced by the backend and the client route is "decoration"), so an expired session still gets 401/403 whatever URL the browser shows. The residue is a refusable/swallowed redirect and a comment-vs-code mismatch: a correctness/UX defect and documentation drift, not a weakened permission gate, secret exposure, injection, or broken crypto check. Not blocking under the Security rubric.
